title: JUDGES ENDS WITH WOMEN BEING SEIZED FOR WIVES—THEN DELIVERS ONE OF THE MOST TERRIFYING VERDICTS IN THE BIBLE: “EVERYONE DID WHAT WAS RIGHT IN HIS OWN EYES.”
paragraphs: JUDGES ENDS WITH WOMEN BEING SEIZED FOR WIVES—THEN DELIVERS ONE OF THE MOST TERRIFYING VERDICTS IN THE BIBLE: “EVERYONE DID WHAT WAS RIGHT IN HIS OWN EYES.”

They called it saving a tribe. But innocent women paid the price. And when the Bible reveals what was happening in Israel, the warning becomes painfully personal: What happens when people still know God's name but no longer surrender to His authority?
There is something deeply disturbing about the final pages of the Book of Judges.
Not because God commanded something cruel.
But because people who belonged to the nation that had received God's Law committed terrible acts while convincing themselves they were solving a problem.
And perhaps the most frightening part is that the story does not end with a dramatic voice from heaven.
No thunder.
No fire.
No prophet stepping forward to announce that everything has been made right.
Instead, the book closes with a sentence that should make every generation examine itself.
“In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.” — Judges 21:25 (KJV)
Read that again.
Not everyone did what was right in God's eyes.
Everyone did what was right in their own eyes.
And immediately before that devastating conclusion, Scripture describes women being taken from a celebration and carried away to become wives.
This was not a romantic love story.
It was not a beautiful biblical marriage ceremony.
It was a nation unraveling.
And the women caught in the middle were not the authors of the disaster.
They were among those who suffered because of it.
What makes this passage so unsettling is that the people involved were not strangers to the things of God.
They were Israelites.
They knew about the covenant.
They knew about the Law.
They knew the history of deliverance from Egypt.
They belonged to a people whose entire existence testified that the Lord had rescued them by His mighty hand.
Yet somehow, in a nation that possessed divine revelation, human judgment had become dangerously detached from divine obedience.
And before we condemn them from the comfortable distance of thousands of years, we need to confront a question.
How many times have we called something right simply because we wanted it badly enough?
How many times have we searched for a religious explanation to defend a decision we had already made?
How many times have we asked God to bless a path we never asked Him to approve?
That is where this ancient story stops feeling ancient.
And begins searching the heart.
The events leading to Judges 21 are among the darkest in the Old Testament.
In Judges 19, a Levite traveling with his concubine arrives in Gibeah, a town belonging to the tribe of Benjamin.
They receive hospitality in the home of an elderly man.
But during the night, violent men surround the house and demand that the Levite be brought outside so they can sexually assault him.
What follows is horrifying.
The woman is sent outside, where she is subjected to sexual violence throughout the night.
By morning, she lies at the doorway.
The narrative presents her as unresponsive, and the following events make clear that she has died.
The Levite then takes her body, divides it into twelve pieces, and sends them throughout Israel.
It is one of the most shocking accounts in Scripture.
And it is important to say something clearly.
The Bible recording an atrocity does not mean the Bible is approving it.
Scripture sometimes shows human evil without softening its brutality because God is not interested in protecting our illusions about what sin can become.
The woman in Judges 19 is not merely a plot device.
She was a human being.
Her suffering mattered.
Her life mattered.
And the terrible way she was treated exposes the moral collapse of the people around her.
The Levite's own actions must not escape scrutiny simply because the narrative begins with the wickedness of the men of Gibeah.
The story forces us to look at a society where the vulnerable could be sacrificed while the powerful continued making decisions.
And the tragedy does not end there.
When Israel hears what happened, the tribes assemble and demand accountability.
Benjamin refuses to surrender the guilty men of Gibeah.
Civil war erupts.
Judges 20 describes devastating battles between Benjamin and the other Israelite tribes.

Israel seeks the Lord during the conflict, and the text records divine direction concerning the fighting. Yet that does not mean every subsequent decision made by the Israelites carries God's approval.
By the end of the war, Benjamin has been nearly destroyed.
Only six hundred Benjaminite men escape to the rock of Rimmon.
Thousands are dead.
Cities have been devastated.
And the surviving Israelites face a terrible realization.
One of their own tribes is on the brink of disappearing.
But another problem has been created by their own oath.
Judges 21:1 records that the men of Israel had sworn at Mizpah that none of them would give his daughter in marriage to a Benjaminite.
Now they mourn the possible disappearance of Benjamin.
They weep before God.
They grieve over the brokenness of Israel.
And yet the solutions they pursue reveal just how deeply compromised their judgment has become.
They discover that Jabesh-gilead had not participated in the national assembly.
An army is sent against the city.
Its inhabitants are killed, except for four hundred young virgins who are taken and given to the surviving Benjaminites.
Even then, there are not enough women for all six hundred men.
So the elders devise another plan.
They know that a yearly festival of the Lord is held at Shiloh.
They instruct the remaining Benjaminite men to hide in the vineyards.
And when the young women of Shiloh come out to dance, the men are told to seize wives for themselves.
Then comes Judges 21:23.

“And the children of Benjamin did so, and took them wives, according to their number, of them that danced, whom they caught: and they went and returned unto their inheritance, and repaired the cities, and dwelt in them.” — Judges 21:23 (KJV)
Consider what that means.
Young women came out to participate in a celebration.
They did not arrive expecting to become the solution to a national crisis.
They were not asked to negotiate the future of a tribe.
They were not given a meaningful choice in the arrangement described.
The men seized them.
And afterward, life in Israel continued.
The Benjaminites returned to their inheritance.
Cities were rebuilt.
Families were reestablished.
But the narrative leaves us with the unsettling reality that a community's restoration had been pursued through the violation of other people's freedom.
The text does not tell us the names of these women.
It does not record their conversations afterward.
It does not describe their private grief or tell us what became of each marriage.
We should not invent details Scripture does not provide.
But we should not pretend that being seized for marriage was an act of loving consent.
A tribe was preserved, but that does not make the means righteous.
And here is where the Hebrew text becomes especially revealing.
Judges 21:23 uses the Hebrew verb וַיִּגְזְלוּ (vayyigzelu), from the root גזל (gazal), meaning to seize, rob, or take by force.
This is not the language of two people freely choosing each other in marriage.
It is the language of taking.
The Hebrew does not invite us to romanticize the event.
It confronts us with its coercive character.
And then, only two verses later, the book ends with its famous verdict.
בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם אֵין מֶלֶךְ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל אִישׁ הַיָּשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו יַעֲשֶׂה
Bayyamim hahem ein melekh beYisra'el; ish hayyashar be'einav ya'aseh.
“In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes.”
The crucial Hebrew expression is הַיָּשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו (hayyashar be'einav).
Literally, it conveys what was right or straight in one's own eyes.
The issue is not simply that people made individual choices.
The issue is that their own judgment had become the measure of righteousness.
They were doing what appeared right to themselves.
And that distinction matters.
Because something can appear necessary and still be wicked.
Something can appear practical and still violate God's commands.
Something can be defended by an entire community and still be unjust.
The elders of Israel had a genuine concern about Benjamin's survival.
But a legitimate concern does not justify an illegitimate solution.
The oath they had made was part of their predicament.
Instead of confronting their own failures with humility, they pursued ways around their oath that left other people bearing the consequences.
Their reasoning may have seemed clever.
Their strategy may have appeared effective.
But effectiveness is not the same as faithfulness.
And the Bible refuses to give us a happy ending simply because the immediate political problem was solved.
Think about how easily this happens in ordinary life.
A husband tells himself that hiding messages from his wife is harmless because nothing physical has happened.
A wife convinces herself that bitterness is justified because she has been wounded.
A pastor begins excusing questionable decisions because the ministry is growing.
A parent humiliates a child and calls it discipline.
A believer refuses to apologize because admitting wrongdoing would damage a reputation carefully maintained for years.
Someone manipulates another person's trust and says it was necessary for a greater good.
And slowly, the conscience learns to cooperate with desire.
Not always through dramatic rebellion.
Sometimes through a thousand small excuses.
One compromise.
One rationalization.
One decision to protect an image instead of telling the truth.
Until eventually, a person can defend what once would have brought them to tears.
That is one of the great dangers exposed by Judges.
Sin does not always announce itself as hatred of God. Sometimes it arrives disguised as a reasonable solution.
And if that does not trouble us, perhaps we have not examined our own hearts closely enough.
But there is another detail we must not overlook.
Judges does not simply say that people did what was right in their own eyes.
It connects this condition to the absence of a king in Israel.
That phrase appears repeatedly throughout the final chapters of the book.
“In those days there was no king in Israel.”
It is part of the book's explanation of Israel's disorder and anticipates the question of kingship that will become central in the books of Samuel.
Yet we must read it carefully.
The Bible does not teach that placing any human ruler on a throne automatically produces righteousness.
Israel's later history proves otherwise.
Many kings would themselves become agents of corruption, idolatry, exploitation, and violence.
A crown cannot cure a sinful heart.
A throne cannot make an unrighteous man holy.
And even Israel's greatest earthly kings would fall short.
The deeper question running through the story is whether God's people will submit to the Lord who rescued them and established His covenant with them.
God had already revealed His will.
The tragedy was not that Israel had received no moral instruction.
The tragedy was that possessing God's instruction had not guaranteed obedience to it.
Deuteronomy 12:8 had warned Israel:
“Ye shall not do after all the things that we do here this day, every man whatsoever is right in his own eyes.” (KJV)
The resemblance is striking.
What Judges describes is precisely the kind of self-directed religious and moral life Israel had been warned against.
And Deuteronomy 16:19 had explicitly condemned the perversion of justice.
God's Law did not give Israel permission to exploit the vulnerable whenever doing so seemed useful.
The Law commanded justice.
The Law restrained human wrongdoing.
The Law revealed the seriousness of sin.
Yet people still found ways to make their own desires sound defensible.
That should humble every Christian who knows the correct vocabulary but struggles to live in obedience.
Because it is possible to quote Scripture while refusing correction.
It is possible to attend worship while hiding cruelty at home.
It is possible to speak passionately about holiness while treating other people as expendable.
It is possible to build a religious reputation while privately resisting the authority of Christ.
Jesus confronted this very danger.
In Matthew 7:21, He declared:
“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.” (KJV)
Notice the warning.
Calling Jesus “Lord” is not the same thing as submitting to Him as Lord.
Religious language is not a substitute for repentance.
Public devotion is not a substitute for private integrity.
And outward success is not proof that every decision behind it was righteous.
Perhaps that is why Judges feels so painfully relevant.
We live in a world where personal preference is often treated as ultimate authority.
If it feels right, do it.
If it makes you happy, pursue it.
If it benefits your future, justify it.
If everyone around you approves, stop asking questions.
But Scripture challenges the assumption that our feelings can safely govern our moral lives.
Proverbs 14:12 warns:
“There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.” (KJV)
The danger is not merely choosing what we know to be wrong.
It is becoming so convinced of our own rightness that we stop listening.
Stop repenting.
Stop examining ourselves.
Stop allowing Scripture to contradict us.
And eventually stop recognizing the damage our choices cause.
There is something especially heartbreaking about the women of Shiloh.
The narrative shows how people with power can make plans while those with less power bear the cost.
The elders had a problem.
The men needed wives.
The oath created an obstacle.
And the proposed solution involved taking women who had not made that oath.
How often has something similar happened across human history?
How often have the vulnerable been told to suffer quietly for the good of a family, an institution, a community, or a religious reputation?
How often has someone been pressured to accept mistreatment because challenging it would make others uncomfortable?
And how often has the language of sacrifice been used to demand something God never commanded?
We must be careful here.
Christian sacrifice is real.
Jesus calls His disciples to deny themselves and follow Him.
But self-denial is not permission for another person to abuse, exploit, or control us.
Submission to Christ does not require calling wickedness righteous.
Forgiveness does not require pretending harm never happened.
And preserving a religious institution is never an excuse for concealing violence or silencing victims.
The God revealed throughout Scripture cares about justice, truth, and the oppressed.
Psalm 82:3 commands:
“Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy.” (KJV)
And Jesus Himself condemned religious leaders who neglected justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
The women in Judges 21 should not disappear from our moral concern merely because the final verse turns our attention to Israel's larger spiritual condition.
Their treatment is part of the evidence of that condition.
The disorder of a society is often revealed by what happens to the people least able to defend themselves.
And that brings us to a question many of us would rather avoid.
Who is paying the price for the decisions we keep defending?
Is it your spouse?
Your children?
Someone who trusted you?
Someone who cannot easily confront you?
Someone whose pain you have minimized because acknowledging it would require you to change?
There are moments when the Holy Spirit uses Scripture not merely to inform us but to expose us.
Not so that we will collapse into hopelessness.
But so that we will stop hiding from the truth.
And perhaps, as you read this, something has already come to mind.
A conversation you have avoided.
A person you have wounded.
A compromise you keep explaining away.
A secret you have become skilled at protecting.
A decision you keep calling necessary, even though your conscience has never been at peace with it.
Please do not rush past that moment.
You do not need to tell strangers the details of your private life.
You do not need to make a public confession that would expose someone else's trauma.
But you can be honest before God.
You can stop defending what He is calling you to surrender.
You can say, even quietly, “Lord, I have been doing what is right in my own eyes.”
And that confession may become the beginning of something beautiful.
Because the Book of Judges does not end with humanity finding the answer.
It ends with humanity exposing its desperate need for one.
And when we read the Bible as a whole, we discover that the answer is greater than merely finding a stronger earthly ruler.
We need a righteous King.
A King who does not exploit the weak to preserve His power.
A King who does not use people as disposable instruments for His own advancement.
A King who does not manipulate justice to protect His reputation.
A King whose righteousness cannot be corrupted.
A King whose mercy does not require pretending evil is good.
And that is where the story points our longing toward Jesus Christ.
Not because Judges 21 explicitly names Jesus.
It does not.
But because the failures of Israel's leaders, the inadequacy of human rule, and the recurring rebellion of God's people reveal a need that finds its ultimate answer in Him.
The promised Son of David.
The righteous Messiah.
The King of kings.
Look at the contrast.
In Judges 21, vulnerable women are seized as part of a plan to preserve a tribe.
In the Gospels, Jesus approaches the broken, the ashamed, the rejected, and the powerless with truth and mercy.
He does not treat them as obstacles to His mission.
He sees them.
He speaks to them.
He restores dignity.
He confronts those who use religion to burden others.
And He gives His own life to save sinners.
That difference should leave us speechless.
Human sin so often says, “Someone else must suffer so I can keep what I want.”
But the Gospel reveals the sinless Son of God willingly giving Himself for people who could never save themselves.
Jesus says in John 10:11:
“I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.” (KJV)
He does not seize the sheep to protect Himself.
He lays down His life for them.
And in John 10:18, Jesus makes clear that His life is not taken from Him against His will.
He lays it down voluntarily.
That matters profoundly.
The cross was not the exploitation of an unwilling victim by a desperate human community.
It was the willing self-offering of the incarnate Son in obedience to the Father, for the salvation of sinners.
This is the heart of the Gospel.
And the Greek New Testament gives us a beautiful expression of this saving grace.
Ephesians 2:8 begins:
Τῇ γὰρ χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι διὰ πίστεως
Tē gar chariti este sesōsmenoi dia pisteōs.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith...” — Ephesians 2:8 (KJV)
The word χάριτι (chariti) comes from χάρις (charis), meaning grace or favor.
And the expression ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι (este sesōsmenoi) emphasizes the state of having been saved through God's gracious action.
Salvation is not something we manufacture by becoming impressive enough.
It is not something we purchase with donations.
It is not a reward for maintaining a flawless religious appearance.
It is God's gift, received through faith.
And Ephesians 2:9 continues:
“Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (KJV)
Do you see the beauty?
The people in Judges kept attempting to solve the consequences of human failure through more human schemes.
But in the Gospel, God accomplishes what sinners cannot accomplish for themselves.
Jesus enters our broken world.
He lives without sin.
He bears our sins in His body on the cross.
He rises from the dead.
And He calls us to repent and believe.
Not to excuse our evil.
Not to baptize our selfishness.
Not to rename our rebellion as freedom.
But to receive forgiveness and be transformed.
That is why the Gospel is so much more than religious encouragement.
It is the announcement that the King we desperately need has come.
And He does not merely improve our outward behavior.
He gives new life.
The prophet Ezekiel recorded God's promise:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you...” — Ezekiel 36:26 (KJV)
This is what we need.
Not simply better excuses.
Not simply stronger willpower.
Not merely a more respectable image.
A new heart.
A heart that learns to love what God loves.
A heart that grieves over sin instead of protecting it.
A heart that values people rather than using them.
A heart that can say, “Lord, even when Your truth confronts my desires, I want Your will more than my own.”
That is the kind of transformation only God's grace can produce.
And perhaps someone reading this has been living with a terrible burden.
You know what it means to be harmed by someone who used religious language to justify wrongdoing.
You know what it means to be told to remain silent for the sake of peace.
You know what it means to feel that your pain mattered less than someone else's reputation.
Please hear this carefully.
What happened to you does not become righteous because someone attached God's name to it.
The Lord is not honored when cruelty is disguised as holiness.
And your worth is not determined by how someone treated you.
You are made in the image of God.
Your life matters.
Your dignity matters.
And while the Bible does not promise that every earthly injustice will be repaired in this lifetime, it does reveal a righteous Judge who will not overlook evil forever.
Jesus Christ is not indifferent to suffering.
He is the crucified and risen Savior who knows what it means to be betrayed, falsely accused, humiliated, and wounded.
His resurrection assures us that death and evil will not have the final word.
Healing may take time.
Justice may require difficult action.
Restoration does not always mean returning to an unsafe relationship.
And forgiveness must never be confused with removing accountability.
But in Christ, suffering does not have to become the final definition of your life.
There is hope beyond what others have done.
There is grace beyond what you have done.
There is redemption for those who turn to Him.
And there is a future that does not have to be governed by yesterday's darkness.
That is why we must understand repentance correctly.
Repentance is not merely feeling bad after being exposed.
It is not a temporary emotional reaction to a powerful message.
It is a turning of the heart toward God, a change of mind that bears fruit in a changed direction.
The Greek word often translated “repent” is μετανοέω (metanoeō).
In Mark 1:15, Jesus proclaims:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.” (KJV)
The Greek command μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite) calls for repentance.
Not merely regret.
Not merely religious excitement.
But a genuine turning in response to God's kingdom and His good news.
And here is something that may change the way you understand surrender.
Repentance is not God demanding that you earn His love by punishing yourself.
It is the appropriate response to His truth and grace.
The same Savior who exposes sin also offers forgiveness.
The same Lord who calls us out of darkness welcomes those who come to Him.
And the same Christ who commands repentance gave Himself to make reconciliation with God possible.
Perhaps you have spent years doing what seemed right in your own eyes.
Perhaps your marriage is suffering because of it.
Perhaps your children have seen a version of Christianity that sounded holy in public but felt harsh at home.
Perhaps your secret compromises have left you exhausted.
Perhaps you have been trying to preserve something that God is asking you to surrender.
Or perhaps you are not the one who caused the harm.
Perhaps you are the one who has been carrying it.
Either way, the answer is not to remain trapped in the final chapter of Judges.
The answer is to come to Jesus.
To bring Him the truth.
To stop pretending.
To confess sin where confession is needed.
To seek protection and justice where harm has occurred.
To make restitution where possible.
To pursue reconciliation where it is safe and appropriate.
And to trust that the grace of Christ is powerful enough to produce a life that looks different from the life we once lived.
Because grace does not merely comfort us while we continue defending sin.
Grace teaches us to renounce it.
Titus 2:11–12 declares:

“For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men, Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world.” (KJV)
Notice that.
Grace teaches.
Grace transforms.
Grace does not leave us celebrating the chains from which Christ came to free us.
And this is where the message becomes deeply personal.
The greatest danger in Judges was not simply that Israel had no human king.
It was that people repeatedly refused to live faithfully under the authority of the God who had already revealed Himself to them.
And today, it is possible to profess Jesus as King while still living as though our own desires occupy the throne.
We can sing about surrender and then refuse to forgive.
We can pray for revival and then resist repentance.
We can ask God to bless our families while refusing to confront the habits destroying them.
We can defend biblical truth online while neglecting love, humility, and integrity offline.
But Jesus is not calling us to perform Christianity.
He is calling us to follow Him.
Even when following Him means admitting we were wrong.
Even when it means abandoning a profitable compromise.
Even when it means apologizing without excuses.
Even when it means refusing to participate in injustice that everyone else has learned to tolerate.
Even when it means choosing faithfulness over popularity.
That is not always easy.
But the alternative is far more dangerous.
Because a heart that continually insists on being its own final authority can become blind to its own destruction.
The people in Judges did not need more creative ways to justify themselves.
They needed to return to the Lord.
And so do we.
There is one more thing about the ending of Judges that I cannot shake.
The book closes after the women have been taken, the tribe has been preserved, and the Israelites have returned to their inheritances.
Outwardly, there is a kind of resolution.
But spiritually, the closing sentence tells us that something is terribly wrong.
The crisis appears to be over.
Yet the deeper sickness remains.
And that is how many people live.
The argument has ended, but the wound remains.
The secret has been hidden, but the guilt remains.
The public scandal has faded, but the unrepentant heart remains.
The family looks normal again, but nobody has addressed what happened.
The ministry keeps growing, but someone is still being hurt.
Everything appears settled.
Except the truth.
And sometimes the most dangerous peace is the peace we manufacture by refusing to confront what is wrong.
Jesus offers something better.
Not the fragile peace of denial.
Not the artificial peace of silence.
But peace with God through His saving work.
Romans 5:1 declares:
“Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.” (KJV)
That peace begins not with our ability to explain ourselves but with Christ's finished work.
And from that reconciliation flows a new way of living.
A way marked by truth.
By justice.
By mercy.
By humility.
By repentance.
By love.
By obedience to the King who gave Himself for us.
Maybe that is what someone needs to hear tonight.
You do not have to keep living under the rule of your worst decisions.
You do not have to keep defending what is destroying you.
You do not have to keep calling darkness light just because you are afraid of what repentance will cost.
And you do not have to believe that your story is beyond redemption.
The cross of Jesus Christ is the place where God's justice and mercy meet.
Sin is not dismissed as insignificant.
Its seriousness is revealed.
And yet sinners are offered forgiveness through the Savior who bore sin and conquered death.
That is grace.
Not permission to remain unchanged.
But mercy that calls us into a new life.
Not because scandal was harmless.
Not because victims should forget.
Not because consequences always disappear.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem sinners, restore what is broken according to His wisdom, and transform lives that once seemed hopeless.
And now I want to ask you something.
Not as a spectator reading an ancient story.
But as someone standing before the living God.
What have you been calling right simply because it was right in your own eyes?
What truth have you been avoiding?
What apology have you been postponing?
What relationship have you been damaging while telling yourself you have good reasons?
What hidden compromise has become so familiar that you barely recognize it anymore?
And if you are the one who has suffered under someone else's wrongdoing, what would it mean to stop accepting their excuses as God's verdict over your life?
These are not questions meant to crush you.
They are invitations to bring your life into the light of Christ.
Because the Gospel does not end with exposure.
It offers redemption.
And no matter how long you have been running, the call of Jesus remains:
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
You can write “Jesus, teach me to surrender” if you are tired of defending your own way.
Or “Christ is still healing me” if you are learning to trust God after deep wounds.
You do not need to reveal private trauma, name someone who harmed you, or disclose a confession that belongs in a safer setting. A simple prayer request is enough.
And if you have a testimony of how Jesus brought you from compromise into repentance, from guilt into forgiveness, or from spiritual darkness into new life, consider sharing it.
Someone reading the comments may need to know that change is possible.
Someone may need to see that surrender is not the end of hope.
It may be the beginning of freedom.
And please, do not let this message stop with you.
You never know who may be scrolling silently.
A father struggling with pride.
A mother carrying exhaustion.
A young believer quietly drifting away from the Lord.
A Christian hiding behind religious activity.
A wounded person wondering whether God sees what happened.
Or someone who has never understood why Jesus came.
Because the goal is not merely to collect readers.
It is to help people encounter the truth of God's Word and grow in faithful obedience to Jesus.
We want to reach more people with the Gospel.
We want to make biblical teaching accessible.
We want to encourage struggling believers, strengthen families, challenge spiritual complacency, and point searching hearts toward Jesus Christ.
And this kind of work takes ongoing commitment, time, and resources.
But I want to be clear about something essential.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
You can pray for this ministry.
You can invite someone to read Scripture.
You can encourage a person who is losing hope.
Those acts of service matter too.
We want biblical nourishment to remain accessible to people who genuinely desire to learn, whether or not they can contribute financially.
These products are not the reason we preach Christ.
The ministry is not your Savior.
Jesus is.
Christ's blood is.
The resources are not the source of eternal life.
The risen Lord is.
Everything we do must lead back to Him.
And as we come to the end of this difficult story, remember where we began.
Women were seized.
A tribe was preserved.
A nation continued.
And Scripture closed with a devastating diagnosis:
Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
The people had found a way to move forward without truly resolving the moral darkness exposed by their actions.
But the Gospel announces that we do not have to remain ruled by that darkness.
There is a King who is perfectly righteous.
A Savior who never exploits the weak.
A Redeemer who calls sinners to repentance.
A Shepherd who lays down His life for His sheep.
A Lord who will judge evil with justice and who offers forgiveness to all who turn to Him in faith.
His name is Jesus Christ.
So do not merely ask whether your choices make sense to you.
Ask whether they honor Him.
Do not merely ask whether your plans are succeeding.
Ask whether they are righteous.
Do not merely ask whether people approve.
Ask whether you are walking in the truth.
And do not allow the final words of Judges to become the final description of your own life.
Let the King reign where self-will once ruled.
Let truth enter where excuses have lived.
Let repentance begin where pride has resisted.
Let grace transform what sin has damaged.
And let Jesus Christ have the final word over your story.
Because the most frightening thing is not that Israel once lived without a righteous king—it is that we can call Jesus our King while still refusing to surrender the throne of our own hearts.
